title: OPPOSITION: GS BIOMATS (003236136)
text:
OPPOSITION DIVISION
OPPOSITION Nо B 3 236 136
Gas Servei, S.A., C/ Motores, 151-156 Naves 8 Y 9, 08038 Barcelona, Spain (opponent),
represented by R. Volart Pons y Cia., S.L., Pau Claris, 77, 2º, 1ª, 08010 Barcelona, Spain
(professional representative)
a g a i n s t
Zhongke Guosheng (Hangzhou) Technology Co., Ltd., 12th Floor, Building 5, No. 20
Longquan Road, Cangqian Street, Yuhang District, 313000 Hangzhou City, Zhejiang
Province, China (holder), represented by Sakellarides Law Offices, 70, Adrianou Street,
10556 Athens, Greece (professional representative).
On 30/07/2026, the Opposition Division takes the following
DECISION:
1. Opposition No B 3 236 136 is upheld for all the contested goods.
2. International registration No 1 832 754 is entirely refused protection in respect of the
European Union.
3. The holder bears the costs, fixed at EUR 620.
REASONS
On 17/03/2025, the opponent filed an opposition against all the goods of international
registration designating the European Union No 1 832 754 ‘GS BIOMATS’ (word mark). The
opposition is based on European Union trade mark registration No 18 187 529
(figurative mark). The opponent invoked Article 8(1)(b) EUTMR.
LIKELIHOOD OF CONFUSION — ARTICLE 8(1)(b) EUTMR
Pursuant to Article 8(1)(b) EUTMR, a likelihood of confusion exists if there is a risk that the
public might believe that the goods or services in question, under the assumption that they
bear the marks in question, come from the same undertaking or, as the case may be, from
economically linked undertakings. Whether a likelihood of confusion exists depends on the
appreciation in a global assessment of several factors, which are interdependent. These
factors include the similarity of the signs, the similarity of the goods and services, the
distinctiveness of the earlier mark, the distinctive and dominant elements of the conflicting
signs, and the relevant public.
a) The goods
The goods on which the opposition is based are the following:

Decision on Opposition No B 3 236 136 Page 2 of 6
Class 1: Chemicals used in industry, science and photography, as well as in agriculture,
horticulture and forestry, in particular refrigerant gases, gas propellents for aerosols,
protective gases for welding and solidified gases for industrial purposes; detergent additives
to petrol [gasoline]; unprocessed artificial resins; unprocessed plastics; manures; fire
extinguishing compositions; tempering and soldering preparations; chemical substances for
preserving foodstuffs; tanning substances; adhesives for use in industry.
The contested goods are the following:
Class 1: Esters; acids; tensio-active agents; diastase for industrial purposes; furfural;
aldehydes; cellulose derivatives [chemicals]; additives, chemical, to motor fuel; biochemical
catalysts; chemical preparations for scientific purposes, other than for medical or veterinary
use.
An interpretation of the wording of the goods or services is required to determine the scope
of protection of these goods or services.
In this respect, the General Court has confirmed that the use of the term ‘in particular’
indicates that the specific goods or services are only examples of items included in the
preceding category and that protection is not restricted to them (09/04/2003, T‑224/01, NU-
TRIDE / TUFFTRIDE, EU:T:2003:107, § 41). In other words, the use of this term in the
specifications of the opponent’s goods only introduces non-exhaustive lists of examples.
The relevant factors relating to the comparison of the goods or services include, inter alia,
their nature, their intended purpose, their method of use and whether they are in competition
with each other or are complementary (‘the Canon criteria’). It is also necessary to take into
account, besides the Canon criteria, other factors, namely distribution channels, the relevant
public and the usual origin of the goods or services (02/06/2021, T‑177/20, Hispano Suiza /
Hispano Suiza, EU:T:2021:312, § 21-22).
The contested goods consist mainly of industrial chemicals, chemical intermediates,
enzymes, catalysts, fuel additives and scientific reagents. They are at least similar to the
opponent’s chemicals used in industry, science, as well as in agriculture, horticulture and
forestry. They coincide, at least, in their relevant public, distribution channels and
commercial origin. Moreover, most of them coincide in their natures, purposes and methods
of use.
b) Relevant public — degree of attention
The average consumer of the category of products concerned is deemed to be reasonably
well informed and reasonably observant and circumspect. It should also be borne in mind
that the average consumer’s degree of attention is likely to vary according to the category of
goods or services in question (22/06/1999, C-342/97, Lloyd Schuhfabrik, EU:C:1999:323, §
26).
In the present case, the goods found to be at least similar target the public at large and
business customers with specific professional knowledge or expertise.
The degree of attention may vary from above-average to high, due to the technical nature,
cost, and specific applications of these goods.
c) The signs

Decision on Opposition No B 3 236 136 Page 3 of 6
GS BIOMATS
Earlier trade mark Contested sign
The relevant territory is the European Union.
The global appreciation of the visual, aural or conceptual similarity of the marks in question
must be based on the overall impression given by the marks, bearing in mind, in particular,
their distinctive and dominant components (11/11/1997, C‑251/95, Sabèl, EU:C:1997:528,
§ 23).
The unitary character of the European Union trade mark means that an earlier European
Union trade mark can be relied on in opposition proceedings against any application for
registration of a European Union trade mark that would adversely affect the protection of the
first mark, even if only in relation to the perception of consumers in part of the European
Union (18/09/2008, C‑514/06 P, ARMAFOAM / NOMAFOAM, EU:C:2008:511, § 57). This
applies by analogy to international registrations designating the European Union. Therefore,
a likelihood of confusion for only part of the relevant public of the European Union is
sufficient to reject the contested application.
The element 'GS', present in both signs, has no meaning for the relevant public and is,
therefore, distinctive to a normal degree.
The contested sign also contains a second element, 'BIOMATS'. Although average
consumers normally perceive a mark as a whole and do not proceed to analyse its various
details, when perceiving a word sign, they will break it down into elements which, for them,
suggest a specific meaning or which resemble words known to them (13/02/2007, T-256/04,
RESPICUR / RESPICORT, EU:T:2007:46, § 57). This is also the case where one part of the
sign has a clear and evident meaning while the rest is meaningless. Bearing the above in
mind, it can be reasonably assumed that the relevant professional public in the whole EU will
readily discern the prefix ‘BIO’ included in the contested sign. According to the case-law, the
use of the verbal element ‘BIO’ as a prefix or suffix has acquired a highly suggestive
connotation and may be perceived in different ways according to the product offered for sale,
but, in general, it refers to the idea of environmental protection, the use of natural materials
or even ecological manufacturing processes (10/09/2015, T-30/14, BIO – INGRÉDIENTS
VÉGÉTAUX – PROPRE FABRICATION (fig.), EU:T:2015:622, § 20). Bearing in mind that
the relevant goods are chemical products and substances that can involve life or living
organisms, or be organic, the common prefix ‘BIO’ is non-distinctive.
As regards the second component ‘MATS', given that the goods at issue consist of various
types of chemicals, and that professionals in the scientific and technical fields are
accustomed to using abbreviations to shorten longer terms, at least the English-speaking
part of the relevant professional public is likely to perceive the component ‘MATS’, preceded
by the prefix ‘BIO’, as an abbreviation of the word ‘material’. Therefore, for that part of the
relevant public, the term, in the context of the goods in Class 1 (chemicals, chemical

Decision on Opposition No B 3 236 136 Page 4 of 6
preparations and biochemical products), is allusive to the nature of the goods, as chemicals
constitute a category of materials. Consequently, it has a weak distinctive character.
Furthermore, for that part of the relevant public, the word ‘BIOMATS’, taken as a whole, will
be understood as conveying the concept of bio-based or biological materials. As it is allusive
to the nature of the goods, namely biological or bio-based chemical materials, it is also, at
best, weakly distinctive.
The likelihood of confusion is more likely to occur for this part of the relevant public, since
the differentiating element is at best of weak distinctive character and, therefore, will thus
have less impact in the overall impression given by the sign. In the light of the above and
taking into account the unitary character of the European Union trade mark, the Opposition
Division finds it appropriate to focus the comparison of the signs on the English-speaking
part of the relevant professional public.
The earlier mark’s verbal element is slightly stylised; however, this stylisation is not
particularly striking, and it will not deviate consumers’ attention from the verbal element itself.
As regards the orange curved swoosh or arc element of the earlier mark, it is a simple
curved decorative shape. The use of such simple arc or swoosh elements is quite common
in trade as a decorative or dynamic device. It is non-distinctive. In any event, when signs
consist of both verbal and figurative components, in principle, the verbal component of the
sign usually has a stronger impact on the consumer than the figurative component. This is
because the public does not tend to analyse signs and will more easily refer to the signs in
question by their verbal element than by describing their figurative elements (14/07/2005, T-
312/03, SELENIUM-ACE / SELENIUM SPEZIAL A-C-E (fig.), EU:T:2005:289, § 37).
The earlier mark has no element that could be considered dominant element (the most eye-
catching).
Consumers generally tend to focus on the beginning of a sign when they encounter a trade
mark (25/03/2009, T‑109/07, SPA THERAPY / SPA, EU:T:2009:81, § 30; 15/12/2009,
T‑412/08, TRUBION / TriBion Harmonis (fig.), EU:T:2009:507, § 40; 06/10/2011, T‑176/10,
SEVEN FOR ALL MANKIND / Seven (fig.) et al., EU:T:2011:577, § 39). This is because the
public reads from left to right, which makes the part placed at the left of the sign (the initial
part) the one that first catches the attention of the reader.
Visually and aurally, the signs coincide in their distinctive element (and its pronunciation)
'GS', which is the sole verbal element of the earlier mark and the first and most distinctive
element of the contested sign. The signs differ in the additional element (and its
pronunciation) 'BIOMATS' of the contested sign, which is at best weak as a whole and
therefore carries limited weight in the overall impression of that sign.
The signs also differ visually in the earlier mark’s slight stylisation and in the orange curved
swoosh, which for the reason explained above will have a very limited impact on consumers.
The applicant argues that the earlier mark is a short mark and the contested sign is
composed of two elements, one of which is much longer. In this regard it should be noted
that the coinciding element, although composed of two letters, constitutes a distinctive and
independent element in both signs. While the differing verbal element ‘BIOMATS’, albeit
much longer, bears a limited weight in the comparison of signs due to its at best weak
distinctive character.
Taken into account everything mentioned above, the signs are visually similar to a below-
average degree and aurally similar to an average degree.

Decision on Opposition No B 3 236 136 Page 5 of 6
Conceptually, reference is made to the previous assertions concerning the semantic
content conveyed by the marks. Whereas the earlier mark is meaningless, the public under
analysis will perceive a concept of ‘bio materials’ in the other one. To that extent, the marks
are conceptually not similar. However, this conceptual difference is of very limited relevance
in the overall comparison of signs, as it stems from an at best weak meaning.
As the signs have been found similar in at least one aspect of the comparison, the
examination of likelihood of confusion will proceed.
d) Distinctiveness of the earlier mark
The distinctiveness of the earlier mark is one of the factors to be taken into account in the
global assessment of likelihood of confusion.
The opponent did not explicitly claim that its mark is particularly distinctive by virtue of
intensive use or reputation.
Consequently, the assessment of the distinctiveness of the earlier mark will rest on its
distinctiveness per se. In the present case, the earlier trade mark as a whole has no
meaning for any of the goods in question from the perspective of the public in the relevant
territory. Therefore, the distinctiveness of the earlier mark must be seen as normal, despite
the presence of a non-distinctive element in the mark, as stated above in section c) of this
decision.
e) Global assessment, other arguments and conclusion
According to the case-law of the Court of Justice, in determining the existence of likelihood
of confusion, trade marks have to be compared by making an overall assessment of the
visual, aural and conceptual similarities between the marks. The comparison ‘must be based
on the overall impression given by the marks, bearing in mind, in particular, their distinctive
and dominant components’ (11/11/1997, C-251/95, Sabel, EU:C:1997:528, § 22). Likelihood
of confusion must be assessed globally, taking into account all the circumstances of the
case.
Likelihood of confusion covers situations where the consumer directly confuses the trade
marks themselves, or where the consumer makes a connection between the conflicting
signs and assumes that the goods/services covered are from the same or economically
linked undertakings (29/09/1998, C‑39/97, Canon, EU:C:1998:442, § 29).
The goods are at least similar. The relevant public consists of the public at large and
business customers, whose degree of attention may vary from above-average to high. The
earlier mark has a normal degree of distinctiveness.
The signs are visually similar to a below-average degree and aurally similar to an average
degree. They are conceptually not similar, although this difference is of very limited
relevance in the overall comparison, as it stems from an at best weak meaning.
The signs coincide in their distinctive element 'GS', which constitutes the sole verbal element
of the earlier mark and the first and most distinctive element of the contested sign. The
additional element 'BIOMATS' of the contested sign, as explained above, is at best weak as
a whole and therefore carries limited weight in the overall impression of the contested sign.
The remaining differences, namely the earlier mark's slight stylisation and its orange curved
swoosh element, are non-distinctive and in any case will not divert consumers' attention from

Decision on Opposition No B 3 236 136 Page 6 of 6
the verbal element. The differences are therefore insufficient to outweigh the similarities
arising from the coincidence in the distinctive element 'GS' and to exclude a likelihood of
confusion.
Indeed, despite the presence of the additional (at best) weak element ‘BIOMATS’ in the
contested sign, it is highly likely that, due to the coincidence in the distinctive verbal element
‘GS’, the relevant public will perceive the contested mark as a sub-brand, a variation of the
earlier mark, configured in a different way according to the type of goods or services that it
designates (23/10/2002, T‑104/01, Fifties / Miss Fifties (fig.), EU:T:2002:262, § 49).
Considering all the above, there is a likelihood of confusion on the part of the English-
speaking part of the relevant professional public. As stated above in section c) of this
decision, a likelihood of confusion for only part of the relevant public of the European Union
is sufficient to reject the contested application.
Therefore, the opposition is well founded on the basis of the opponent’ EUTM registration No
18 187 529. It follows that the contested trade mark must be rejected for all the contested
goods.
COSTS
According to Article 109(1) EUTMR, the losing party in opposition proceedings must bear the
fees and costs incurred by the other party.
Since the holder is the losing party, it must bear the opposition fee as well as the costs
incurred by the opponent in the course of these proceedings.
According to Article 109(1) and (7) EUTMR and Article 18(1)(c)(i) EUTMIR, the costs to be
paid to the opponent are the opposition fee and the costs of representation, which are to be
fixed on the basis of the maximum rate set therein.

According to Article 67 EUTMR, any party adversely affected by this decision has a right to
appeal against this decision. According to Article 68 EUTMR, notice of appeal must be filed
in writing at the Office within two months of the date of notification of this decision. It must be
filed in the language of the proceedings in which the decision subject to appeal was taken.
Furthermore, a written statement of the grounds for appeal must be filed within four months
of the same date. The notice of appeal will be deemed to have been filed only when the
appeal fee of EUR 720 has been paid.
